pacify

/PAS-uh-fy/ - the stress falls on PAS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Pacify means to calm the anger or agitation of someone.

A new fence, a written apology, and a crate of apples finally pacified the neighbor whose garden the goats had ruined.

Example

When the library announced late fines would double, a patron marched to the desk with her card raised like a warrant, voice climbing with every sentence. The librarian let her finish, waived the disputed fine on the spot, and showed her the new amnesty week in the calendar. Pacified, the patron renewed her card before she left.

Pacify is the right verb because its target is an angry person, and success means restoring peace. Its cluster-mate allay would suit her fears, not her fury — you allay a worry with facts, but you pacify a person who is already boiling.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

settle: To settle is to bring a dispute or unrest to rest, and its object can be anything — an argument, a lawsuit, a jittery market. Pacify aims squarely at a person or crowd whose anger is already up. You settle the quarrel itself; you pacify the furious neighbor it produced.

disarm: To disarm is to melt someone's anger or suspicion away by charm, humor, or a surprising confession — the hostility dissolves rather than being talked down. Pacify is broader and more workmanlike: apologies, concessions, repairs, whatever restores the peace. A well-timed joke disarms; an apology and a fair offer pacify.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

enrage: to push someone into fury

agitate: to stir a person or crowd into unrest

Where it sits · how much force the calming takes

soothe → pacify → subdue

soothe vs. pacify: Soothing eases discomfort gently — a lullaby, a cool cloth; pacify goes further, taking someone already angry back down to peace.

subdue vs. pacify: Subdue goes beyond pacify: the pacified crowd chooses to calm down, while a subdued one has been overpowered into quiet.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — pac: peace (Latin pax, pacis)

Suffix — -ify: to make

Put it together: Pac (peace) + -ify (to make) = to make peaceful. Latin pax gave English its whole peace family, and pacify is its working verb: whatever the anger — a customer, a crowd, a border region — to pacify it is to manufacture peace where there was none.

Use the root in a new word: pacifist: A lifelong pacifist, she marched against every war her country entered.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Pacify points at an angry or agitated someone — a toddler, a customer, a province — and means bringing them back to peace, sometimes with an edge of mere quieting rather than true fixing. Use allay when the object is the fear or concern itself, and soothe when the trouble is discomfort rather than anger.
